title: Electrochemical reduction of CO2 to synthesis gas on CNT supported CuxZn1-x O catalysts
abstract: Electrochemical CO2 reduction is a promising method for the production of CO2 neutral fuels and chemicals from renewable electricity. ZnO supported on CNT is a low-cost electro catalyst that can produce syngas from CO2 and H2O. A rational catalyst design strategy for further improvement of the ZnO/CNT catalyst is to dope with copper to strengthen the binding energy of the CO intermediate, which could improve the activity. In this work, a series of CuZnO/CNT catalysts with intimate Cu and Zn contact and various Cu loadings are prepared. By varying the copper content we show that the synergy of copper and zinc improves the activity for CO formation, and the optimal copper content is 20 at%. On hydrogen evolution, the addition of copper has a two-fold effect. This reaction is enhanced by the reduced ZnO particle size obtained when copper is added, but at similar particle sizes of ZnO, a suppression is observed with increasing copper content as CO evolution is enhanced. Stability tests showed that pure ZnO phase is more stable than metallic copper on ZnO. Compared with polycrystalline silver, the CuZnO/CNT catalysts are more active for syngas formation at a useful CO: H2 composition. This work demonstrates that the viability of DFT based rational design of electrochemical CO2 reduction catalyst. By varying CuZnO composition as well as crystallite size, one is able to tune the electrochemical reduction activity towards CO and H2, and therefore achieve desired syngas ratio.

Electrochemical reduction of CO2 to synthesis gas on CNT supported CuxZn1x O catalysts
Ida Hjortha, Magnus Nordb, Magnus Rønninga, Jia Yanga,⁎, De Chena,⁎
a Department of Chemical Engineering, Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU), Sem Sælands vei 4, NO-7491, Trondheim, Norway bUniversity of Glasgow, School of Physics and Astronomy, Glasgow, G12 8SU, United Kingdom
A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords: Electrochemical CO2 reduction Hydrogen evolution Catalysis Carbon nanotubes Copper Zinc
A B S T R A C T
Electrochemical CO2 reduction is a promising method for the production of CO2 neutral fuels and chemicals from renewable electricity. ZnO supported on CNT is a low-cost electro catalyst that can produce syngas from CO2 and H2O. A rational catalyst design strategy for further improvement of the ZnO/CNT catalyst is to dope with copper to strengthen the binding energy of the CO intermediate, which could improve the activity. In this work, a series of CuZnO/CNT catalysts with intimate Cu and Zn contact and various Cu loadings are prepared. By varying the copper content we show that the synergy of copper and zinc improves the activity for CO formation, and the optimal copper content is 20 at%. On hydrogen evolution, the addition of copper has a two-fold effect. This reaction is enhanced by the reduced ZnO particle size obtained when copper is added, but at similar particle sizes of ZnO, a suppression is observed with increasing copper content as CO evolution is enhanced. Stability tests showed that pure ZnO phase is more stable than metallic copper on ZnO. Compared with polycrystalline silver, the CuZnO/CNT catalysts are more active for syngas formation at a useful CO: H2 composition. This work demonstrates that the viability of DFT based rational design of electrochemical CO2 reduction catalyst. By varying CuZnO composition as well as crystallite size, one is able to tune the electrochemical reduction activity towards CO and H2, and therefore achieve desired syngas ratio.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
A demand for energy storage solutions is prompted by the investments in renewable, but intermittent, electrical energy sources, which has become market leading. Electrochemical CO2 reduction (ECR) into liquid fuels is a promising strategy bridging such energy storage and carbon-neutral energy carriers, as it provides a mean of storing renewable electricity in a convenient, high-density form [1,2]. However, CO2 is the most stable molecule and activation of CO2 molecules is extremely challenging, resulting in a requirement of large over potential. Copper is currently the most studied catalyst for electrochemical CO2 reduction, due to the unique activity for hydrocarbon (C1-C3) formation [3]. The main drawback is that the yields and concentrations of products are too low, increasing separation cost. Consequently electrochemical CO2 conversion is currently neither efficient nor economic [4]. Moreover, simultaneous hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) in aqueous electrolytes is almost inevitable during the ECR, leading to a low Faradaic efficiency for the targeted hydrocarbons. As an alternative, combined ECR and HER to simultaneously produce synthesis gas (CO+H2) has attracted an increasing attention [5,6]. Syngas is a
valuable platform feedstock for liquid fuel/chemical production such as well-established methanol synthesis and Fischer-Tropsch synthesis.
Great efforts have been devoted to the development of ECR electrocatalysts for various products formation [7–11]. Not only the activity but also the selectivity depends significantly on the identity of the transition metals. Among various catalysts reported, only Au and Ag give high selectivity to CO [5,12]. Copper is unique among transition metals, which can produce a wide range of products, including CO, formate, hydrocarbons, and alcohols, depending on the conditions. Recently, zinc, is also found to show high selectivity for synthesis gas (syngas) and CO [13–15]. The oxidation state of Zn and crystal facet of Zn could influence the CO2 reduction efficiency to CO [14,15]. Considering the cost and commercialization potential, Cu or Zn based systems are promising CO2 reduction catalysts for syngas production. The selectivity depends on the catalyst composition. Albo et al. found that Cu2O/ZnO catalyst give enhanced selectivity to methanol and higher stability in CO2 reduction [16,17]. Qin et al. reported the influence of crystal facet of Zn on the CO2 reduction selectivity. They found that Zn (101) facet favor formation of CO while Zn (002) crystal facet favor H2 evolution reaction. A faradaic efficiency (FE) of 85% at

-0.9 V (vs. RHE) for syngas was achieved with catalyst containing more (101) facets. In order to provide more insights and guide the development of CO2 conversion catalyst, density functional theory has been used to calculate the binding energies of key intermediates. Kuhl et al. found a volcano trend between the binding energy of CO and the metal activity of ECR on seven transition metal catalysts, where gold has been shown to have the maximal current density for ECR at -0.8 V with an optimal CO binding energy [3]. The Cu and Zn catalysts were reported to have the stronger and weaker CO adsorption strength than Au, respectively. Catalyst alloy is a typical strategy to tune the binding energies for intermediates in ECR [18] and lower the cost of catalysts. A DFT study showed Cu3Zn and Zn3Cu are more active for CO formation than Cu, and Zn3Cu even showed better activity than the more expensive gold catalyst [19]. Furthermore, the binding of CO on ZnO is slightly stronger than to Zn [20], suggesting ZnO as a possible better ECR catalyst for CO formation. Therefore, alloying ZnO with Cu could potentially improve the activity for CO formation. In addition, Cu metal binds protons more strongly compared to Zn metal, and has a higher activity for HER [21,22]. Combing Cu with ZnO and tuning the composition of the two, one is able to control the HER/ECR activity. As a result, more favourable H2/CO ratio can be obtained, suitable for downstream value-adding processes.
The Cu-ZnO system supported on alumina has been used for industrial scale methanol synthesis from synthesis gas (CO2 + CO + H2→CH3OH) for decades. The unique activity of Cu-ZnO for methanol synthesis from CO2 is due to synergetic Cu-Zn alloy surface sites [23,24], where the oxyphilic Zn atom stabilizes the oxygen atom in CO2, thus improves the binding of the intermediate. The highest reaction rates for methanol synthesis are found when the copper surface is Zn-rich [25,26] and surface is in highly dynamic response to the environment [27]. Under strong reducing conditions Cu exhibits "wetting" behaviour on ZnO, and metallic Zn atoms migrate to the Cu surface [28] although the reducibility of ZnO is low. It is therefore of interest to maximize the contact between the copper and zinc on the catalyst surface, as well as control the composition.
In this work, we explore cost effective CNT supported CuxZn1-xO oxide as bifunctional catalysts to catalyze both ECR and HER reactions generating synthesis gas with controllable H2/CO ratios. The relationship between composition, structure, properties and electrochemical performance of catalysts in terms of catalyst activity and selectivity (H2/CO ratio) is addressed.

sections.heading: 2.1. Catalyst synthesis
sections.text:
Commercial MWCNTs from Chengdu were purified and oxidized by heating in HNO3 at reflux conditions. The fibers were treated 3 times for 2 h, and washed with distilled water. The purified fibers were dried at 110 °C overnight, and mortared into a powder.
ZnO/CNT and CuxZn1-xO/CNT was prepared by incipient wetness impregnation of the acid treated CNTs with a polymerizable metalcomplex solution, containing copper nitrates, citric acid and ethylene glycol [29]. Cu(NO3)2..3H2O and Zn(NO3)2.6H2O precursors were used. The Zn/Cu ratio was varied, while keeping sum of the molar loading on carbon constant. A 1:1:1 ratio of (Cu+Zn), citric acid and ethylene glycol was dissolved in distilled water and immediately impregnated on the CNTs.
After drying overnight at 110 °C, the samples were calcined under 10 vol%O2/N2 flow. The oven was ramped 2 K/min to the target temperature and kept at the calcination temperature (300 °C or 350 °C) for 2 h. Then, the oven was set to the reduction temperature and the reactor was purged with argon before the flow of H2 was introduced. The samples were reduced under H2 flow for 5 h, cooled to room temperature and passivated for 2 h with 0.5 vol% O2 in Ar. Details about nominal catalyst composition and calcination, as well as reduction
temperature are given in Table 1. A set of catalysts were also prepared by standard impregnation of copper nitrate aqueous solution on ZnO/CNT for comparison. Catalysts used for stability measurements were prepared by incipient wetness impregnation of copper nitrate salt on ZnO/CNT.

sections.heading: 2.2. Characterization
sections.text: The copper-zinc oxide coated CNTs were imaged with a Hitachi S5500 STEM microscope, in Bright Field (BF), Annular Dark Field (ADF) and Secondary Electron (SE) imaging mode. Energy Dispersive X- ray Spectroscopy (EDS) data was also recorded for some samples. To maximize the EDS and HAADF signal, high probe currents were used. This could lead to problems with carbon contamination, so beam showers were sometimes performed to reduce this. In addition, the STEM samples were usually kept at 60 °C in a vacuum oven overnight before the measurement. These samples were prepared by dispersing catalyst powder in alcohol by ultra-sonication, and a droplet of this ink was dropped onto TEM-grids of gold with carbon film. Measurements of copper particle sizes were done in ImageJ software. Three catalysts were also examined with STEM-EELS, in a probe corrected JEOL ARM 200 cF, and the data were analysed with HyperSpy. The data was treated with principle component analysis (PCA), the power law background was subtracted, and Hartree-Slater cross sections were used to plot the signal from Zn-L2,3 and Cu-L2,3. X-ray diffractograms were recorded with a Bruker D8 Advance DaVinci X-ray Diffractometer with a MoK source, in variable slit mode. By using Rietveldt refinement in Topas, lattice parameters and crystallite sizes were calculated for the zincite phase. The BET surface area was measured in a Micrometrics Tristar II 3020 BET apparatus, using typically 70–100mg sample.

sections.heading: 2.3. Electrochemcial testing
sections.text:
A 49×49mm glassy carbon current collector plate was cleaned and polished with a fine cloth and alumina slurry, washed with water and isopropanol. The desired amount of catalyst powder was weighed and 2–3mL isopropanol was added per mg of catalyst. The catalyst loading on the glassy carbon electrode is shown in Table S1 in the supporting information. All catalyst inks were prepared by dispersing the catalyst powder in isopropanol by ultra-sonication until the solution looked uniform. Then, the ink was sprayed on the clean glassy carbon current collector with an airbrush. The electrode was mounted on the cell. For the measurements, an Ag/AgCl electrode was used as the reference electrode. A 0.1M KHCO3 electrolyte was used. Ultrapure KHCO3 from Sigma Aldrich was dissolved in deionized water and used as catholyte. A KHCO3 of 99.9% purity was used as anolyte. The electrolyte was vigorously purged with CO2 for 10 (anolyte) and 5
(catholyte) minutes, long enough for the pH to stabilize [30]. Immediately after saturation with CO2, the electrolyte was injected with a large syringe in the anolyte and catholyte compartments, while 10mL/ min CO2 was bubbled through the compartments. This bubbling was kept constant during the subsequent measurement, and lead to turbulent mixing of the electrolyte close to the cathode. To avoid corrosion under open circuit conditions, the measurement was started immediately after injecting the catholyte. A stepped chronopotentiometric program was executed. The cell was kept for 30min at a constant reduction current, and then the reduction current was increased. In between the steps a short impedance measurement was performed, to determine the solution resistance for correction of the iR-drop. A microGC was used to analyse the gaseous products, and Ar was used as internal standard to determine the product flow. Gaseous samples were analysed approximately every 3min. sections.heading: 3.1.1. ZnO crystal structure and catalyst morphology
sections.text:
A series of CuZnOCNT catalysts was successfully prepared. Nominal loading was achieved for most of the catalysts verified by thermal gravimetric analysis (Table S2). To ensure good electrical conductivity, highly dispersed copper and zinc with intimate contact were deposited on carbon nanotubes (CNTs) [29,32]. Moreover, the mesoporous structure of the CNTs can enhance mass transfer compared to microporous materials [33–35], which is especially important for good performance of applications with gas diffusion electrodes [36]. The X-ray diffractograms of the reduced and passivated sample revealed the presence of a ZnO phase with a hexagonal wurtzite structure. Lattice parameters and crystallite sizes for the ZnO phase were extracted. In the catalysts with a high copper amount (> 14%), a metallic copper phase was also observed. We will discuss copper phase segregation later. The relationship between the ZnO lattice parameters (a, c, u), copper fraction and crystallite size is plotted in Fig. 1. Where a(ZnO) is the interatomic distance between cations in the crystallographic planes containing only cations (zinc), c(ZnO) is the direction of the polar axis of the ZnO unit cell as shown in Fig. 1c. u(ZnO) is internal parameter, which can be calculated by Eq 3.

Fig. 1a shows that as copper content increase to 25%, the lattice parameter a is compressed for the same group of samples prepared with co-impregnation, calcined and reduced at 300 °C (red circle). This is possibly due to the replacement of smaller radius Cu2+ atoms into ZnO lattice. However, a(ZnO) increased back to the level of pure ZnO when Cu loading is at 50%, possibly due to Cu segregation at high loading. This is consistent with literature showing that up to 5–10 % substitution of Zn by Cu yielded reduced ZnO lattice parameters [37,38], owing to slightly smaller ionic radius of Cu2+ compared with Zn2+ [39].
In addition to the compression of a(ZnO) with increasing copper substitution, we observe a simultaneous reduction in the lattice parameter c(ZnO) for crystallites with similar size (Table S3). The c(ZnO) lattice parameter, which is in the direction of the polar axis of the ZnO unit cell, has a strong correlation with the crystallite size. The increase in c with decreasing particle size has also been observed by Ghosh et al. [40].
Internal parameter u-value can be calculated from a(ZnO) and c (ZnO) and a decreasing u-value is related to an increasing particle aspect ratio. The change in u(ZnO) with decreasing crystalline size shown in Fig. 1b therefore indicate that the ZnO phase undergoes a shape transition when going from large to small crystallite sizes. ZnO particles usually grow with the c-planes perpendicular to the CNT substrate [41], so the expansion and change in u-value indicates that the particles with small crystallite size have a better wetting of the carbon support.
Particle morphology was studied with STEM, which corroborated the above hypothesis as images showed very small particles coating the CNT more like a film layer. The size of the particles from STEM images were analysed, and particles from 4 to 5 nm and larger could be measured accurately. For smaller particles, the accurate size could not be measured due to limited spatial resolution, so a size range is given. The mean size, standard deviation and number of measured particles are summarized in Table S1 in Supporting information, together with the calculated crystallite size.
Key observations are shown in Fig. 2. The Cu14Zn86O/CNT catalyst calcined and reduced at 300 °C shows very small particles, covering the tubes like a film. However, larger particles were also observed in STEM, and the particle size distribution is bimodal. The same catalyst, when reduced at 350 °C, it seems like the larger particles have become smaller, and the film like structure has broken up and grown into small particles, resulting in unimodal distribution with average particle size of 7 nm. In addition, the crystallite size of ZnO has been calculated by Scherrer equation. For the sample reduced at 300 °C, the crystallite size from XRD is larger than the particles seen in STEM. When the reduction temperature increased to 350 °C, there is a much better compliance between the crystallite size and STEM particle size. This is because Xray analysis will only probe the crystalline population of the particles and those particles with crystallite size larger than ca. 5 nm. The same effect is also found for the Cu8Zn92O/CNT catalyst. When reduced at 300 °C, the size distribution is clearly bimodal. At the reduction temperature of 350 °C, the distribution is unimodal with average particle size of around 7 nm. In both cases, the relative population of the two size groups is difficult to establish.
Overall, it is demonstrated that when sufficient amounts of copper are added, the ZnO phase wets the surface better and the particle size is smaller, forming a film like structure over CNT. This structure has lower crystallinity possibly due to small crystallite size. In addition to this layer, some of the catalysts have a population of larger crystalline particles. These are probably resilient in the mild reduction condition of 300 °C. At higher reduction temperature of 350 °C, the film forms particles, and the larger particles break up into smaller ones, resulting in unimodal particle size distribution, as shown in Figure S1 in the Supporting information.

sections.heading: 3.1.2. Copper segregation
sections.text:
Copper segregates as a separate phase at sufficiently high copper fractions. Different solubilities of Cu in ZnO have been reported in the literature. Experimental results have shown onset of copper segregation to the grain boundaries happens at 5–10 at%, depending on synthesis procedure [37,38,42,43]. In current study, we observe that in general the crystallinity of the ZnO phase is worse with higher Cu content. Fig. 3a shows the X-ray diffractogram for Cu8Zn92O/CNT reduced at 300 °C. Carbon, ZnO and Ni phases are identified, and these peaks are also representative for the other catalysts. The formation of a metallic copper phase with the addition of copper is closely studied in Fig. 3b-d). At 50 at% copper, the (111) and (200) reflections of cubic metallic
copper is clearly seen, in Fig. 3b and c respectively. Weak copper reflections can also be seen for 25 and 14 at% copper. At 8 and 10 at%, there is no significant change in the diffractogram compared to the copper-free ZnO/CNT reference. Thus, we conclude that at above 10% copper, there is Cu segregation from CuxZn1-xO/ CNT. Catalyst reduction conditions also influence the interaction of copper phase with ZnO, as shown by Fig. 3d for Cu14Zn86O/CNT reduced at 300 °C and 350 °C, respectively. A slight shift of Cu(111) to the left suggests that more zinc is alloyed with the copper phase, at the higher reduction temperature. It is known that increasing the reduction temperature leads to more diffusion of Zn to the Cu phase [28], and ZnO/Zn can also migrate to the copper surface [25,44]. Due to overlap of the Cu(111) and CNT X-ray reflections in samples with Cu as a minority constituent, a quantitative analysis of the copper metallic phase from X-ray is difficult. XRD data for samples with different Cu loading are shown in Figure S2 in the supporting information. To further investigate the segregation of copper, Cu25Zn75O/CNT, Cu14Zn86O/CNT and Cu10Zn90O/CNT reduced at 300 °C were examined with STEM and Electron Energy Loss Spectroscopy (EELS). Elemental maps of zinc and copper for Cu25Zn75O/CNT and Cu14Zn86O/CNT are shown in Fig. 4. Distinct copper rich particles are clearly seen in Cu25Zn75O/CNT (Fig. 4a). No copper rich regions were found on Cu14Zn86O/CNT and Cu10Zn90O/CNT. In these samples, the profiles of the copper and zinc edges are similar, as shown in Fig. 4b, which suggests that copper is evenly distributed on and in ZnO. It is consistent with the observation that ZnO stabilizes the dispersion of copper [45]. Furthermore, the intensity of the Zn edge is 10 times higher than the intensity of Cu. Although absolute quantification should be done with care, an estimation of the concentration of copper associated with zinc can be still made. The scattering cross sections of Zn and Cu are quite similar [46], and this is therefore an indication that the Zn:Cu ratio is approximately 10. More HAADF-EELS data for the 3 samples are shown in Figure S3-S6 in the Supporting information.

sections.heading: 3.2. Electrochemical CO2 reduction in aqueous phase
3.2.1. Synthesis gas formation
sections.text:
The catalysts were tested for electrochemical CO2 reduction in 0.1 M KHCO3. Gaseous products were monitored by a GC. H2 and CO were the main products, but CH4 and a trace amount of C2H4 were also formed on Cu50Zn50O/CNT. Liquid products were not analysed. All catalysts were tested using the procedure described in the experimental section. The partial CO and H2 currents for CuxZn1-xO/CNT catalysts reduced
at 300 and 350 °C are shown in Fig. 5. A general trend is that the onset of CO evolution is slightly before the onset of H2 evolution, but at increasing overpotential the H2 evolution takes over, and CO evolution declines. Same electrochemical reduction experiment has been performed without the presence of CO2. H2 formation was observed but no CO formation occurred (Figure S7), confirming that the CO is indeed a product of CO2 reduction. Due to the relatively low potential, high zinc to copper ratio, small amount of metallic Cu and absence of Cu2O, the methanol selectivity is expected to be very low [3,16] and ethanol selectivity should be below 10% for all the catalysts. For metallic Zn based catalyst, CO and H2 were reported to be the major products, with small amount of formate [47,48], while ZnO only produces CO and small amount of H2 [49,50]. At the two most negative potentials for each catalyst, it was observed that the CO formation declined during the 30min segment. First a small decline, and then a substantial decline at the most negative potential.
Here, CO formation cannot be considered as steady state. Nafion membranes are not only permeable to protons, but also to other cations such as K+ [51]. Analysis of the used catholyte revealed doubling of the K+ concentration during the ECR measurement program. This explains the reduction in solution resistance observed in Figure S8, and indicates that the pH of the catholyte increased over the course of the measurement. Most of the increase can be attributed to the segments with the largest overpotential, where the rates of OH− formation is highest.
The H2/CO ratio is of special interest for further utilization of the syngas mixture in the Fischer-Tropsch process. Therefore, the syngas composition produced by Cu/CNT, ZnO/CNT and Cu14Zn86O/CNT (reduced at 350 °C) is studied in Fig. 6. Firstly, the higher overall activity on the Cu/CNT catalyst at relatively low potentials (Fig. 6b) is due to an enhanced H2 formation where the H2/CO ratio is about 50 (Fig. 6a). The two Zn-containing catalysts show a very different behaviour. They have lower overall activity compared to Cu/CNT (Fig. 6a), but the selectivity and activity for CO is higher. CO formation is slightly higher than H2 formation, down to -0.9 V. At more negative voltage than this, the H2/CO ratio of syngas increases, due to the inhibition of CO formation. Measurements were also done using only oxidized CNTs as catalyst. The pure CNT support has much less activity for HER than both Cu/CNT and ZnO/CNT, as seen in Figure S9. Bare carbon surface on the Cu/CNT catalysts is therefore not the cause of the high HER activity of Cu/CNT. The reproducibility of the ECR and HER measurement is shown in Figure S10 in the Supporting information.
The energy and faradaic efficiency for all catalysts were studied as a function of potential, Figure S11. Cu14Zn86O/CNT and Cu50Zn50O/CNT

catalysts represent well some general trends and are shown in Fig. 7. For the rest of the catalysts, energy and faradaic efficiency is shown in the Supporting information. Cu50Zn50O/CNT is the only catalyst with significant methane formation, and also trace levels of C2H4 (faradaic efficiency< 1%). On contrary to the Cu14Zn86O/CNT catalyst, this catalyst has a metallic crystalline copper nanoparticle phase. Studies on size-dependency of CO2 reduction on copper have shown that larger nanoparticles are needed for significant hydrocarbon formation [52]. Although 5 nm and smaller Cu particles show an increase in activity, this is mostly due to the improved H2 formation and shifted selectivity from hydrocarbons to CO [52].On well dispersed Cu, as the Cu14Zn86O/ CNT catalyst, hydrocarbon formation is therefore suppressed. On crystalline copper, selectivity for CH4 versus C2H4 is structure sensitive [53]. The low selectivity for C2H4 indicates that the emerged copper phase on Cu50Zn50O/CNT mainly exposes planes where ethylene formation is inactive. Hydrocarbon formation was not observed on the pure Cu/CNT catalyst tested in Fig. 6. Indeed, hydrocarbon formation was observed on Cu/CNT catalysts at higher overpotentials in stronger
electrolytes, but the ECR stability was very low (Figure S12) and HER dominating. On copper foil, these products forms mainly at potentials more negative than −0.9 V [54], thus outside the measurement range in Fig. 6.
Cu14Zn86O/CNT represent well the catalysts without a crystalline copper phase, in terms of the range in which energy and faradaic efficiency lie. The range of faradaic efficiencies for syngas is 80–90%. This is comparable to silver-based catalysts [12,55], and better than copper catalysts [54,56]. Table 2 compares the pure ZnO/CNT and the best performing Cu14Zn86O/CNT catalyst with polycrystalline silver [57] and other Zn based catalysts [47,49,58] for syngas production. The performance of the ZnO/CNT already equals the silver catalyst [57], and addition of 14 at% copper further improves the activity. At a lower overpotential, the reaction rate for 1:1 syngas is 15% higher when Cu is added. In addition, the Cu14Zn86O/CNT catalyst outperforms the ZnO and Zn nanoparticles catalyst in the Table 2. A most recent work of an oxygen-vacant-poor ZnO catalyst showed slightly higher current density at slightly lower overpotential [49]. Overall, the CuZnO/CNT
Fig. 2. STEM image of a) Cu14Zn86O/CNT calcined at 300 °C and 350 °C respectively, and histogram of particle size distribution derived from STEM image. b) Cu8Zn92O/CNT calcined at 300 °C and 350 °C respectively, and histogram of particle size distribution derived from STEM image.
catalyst family show relative high activity as well as high flexibility in tuning syngas composition. The formation rate of the Cu14Zn86O/CNT catalyst is 28 umol/g.s for both CO and H2, respectively. If the rate is normalized to the BET surface area, the rate is equal to 0.37 umol/m2.s. This rate is relative low compared with literature data. This is possibly because the surface area here is based on BET surface area of the catalyst material loaded instead of the geometric surface area of the electrode. Despite the difference in active surface area of a foil and supported nanoparticles, this comparison demonstrates the promising potential of the CuZnO/CNT catalyst family. The major advantage of the CuZnO-based catalyst is the lower cost over silver and gold.

sections.heading: 3.2.2. Composition and particle size dependence of activities
sections.text:
Copper has an effect on the performance of the catalyst. Fig. 6 showed clearly that Cu addition enhances the activity of a ZnO/CNT catalyst. In addition, the selectivity for CO is much higher for the ZnOcontaining catalysts compared to the Cu/CNT catalyst. A volcano-curve can be seen for CO formation at -0.9 V with respect to the fraction of copper in the material (Fig. 8a). Given the enhanced electrolyte mixing
from the CO2 bubbling, at this relatively low potential and reaction rate, external mass transfer is assumed to be negligible. The CO partial current increases with increasing Cu content and reaches a maximum at about 20% Cu. Beyond this copper amount, the CO partial current decreases. At these high copper amounts, a significant amount of metallic copper nanoparticles forms in the material. As seen for Cu/CNT and Cu50Zn50O/CNT, Cu nanoparticles are more active for H2 formation, and also for hydrocarbon formation, Figure S12. Protons bind more favourably to Cu than Zn, making it a more active HER catalyst [22]. The insert in Fig. 8a represents a volcano curve for ECR activity with the CO binding energy as descriptor, with literature values for metallic zinc, silver, gold and copper [3]. CO binds more strongly to ZnO than Zn and the binding strength to ZnO is somewhere between silver and gold [20]. From this volcano plot, it is therefore predicted that the oxidation of zinc will enhance ECR. More importantly, the prediction is in good agreement with the experimental observation where ZnO/CNT is more active for CO evolution than the Cu/CNT reference. Based on the CO binding energy, the copper and ZnO located on the right and left sides in of the volcano curve, respectively. Thus, the addition of copper

(b) and (c) compares the main metallic copper reflections (111) and (200) for materials with varying copper content, reduced at 300 °C. (d) The effect of reduction temperature on Cu(111) of Cu14Zn86OCNT.
to zinc oxide can push the activity further up to the top of the volcano. As CO2 adsorbs to ZnO through the oxygen [59], a possible role for a neighboring Cu could be to bind the carbon in COOH*. It might point out the new active sites for ECR on Cu-ZnO catalysts. The synergy is similar to what is found for industrial methanol synthesis catalysts [23,24]. Moreover, in natural photosynthesis, CO2 activation occurs also by a combination of nucleophilic and electrophilic attacks on the carbon and oxygen atom, respectively [60]. In addition, adding copper to ZnO improves electrical conductivity [37,61], reflected by the reduced resistance of the catalysts with increasing Cu contents in the impedance spectroscopy in Figure S8.
The analysis of H2 evolution for the different materials does not give a clear correlation with copper content (Fig. 8b), as the H2 evolution shows a clear CuZnO size dependency (Fig. 8d). Below 20 nm, the uvalue of ZnO decreased monotonically with crystallite size, which indicated a shape transition where the particles are elongated in the cdirection, had a better wetting of the carbon support and a tendency for film formation. The improved HER activity on smaller crystallite size (down to 5–6 nm) might be due to more low coordinated ZnO sites which can favor water adsorption and dissociation. Water dissociation is regarded as a structure sensitive reaction which is favoured by a smaller particle size [62,63]. Due to a thinner oxide layer, the electrical conductivity is also potentially improved, which also will improve activity. The activity of the uncoated support is much lower than the activity of the ZnO-based catalysts (Figure S9), and also not particularly selective for HER. Thus, the difference in H2 activity is not likely to be due to more exposed carbon surface. On the contrary, the poorer wetting by the larger particles will give a smaller ZnO surface. CO evolution is not as sensitive to the particle size as H2 evolution. Little difference in activity is observed as the ZnO particle size is reduced (Figure S13). On
copper electrocatalysts, it is shown that CO2 reduction is structure sensitive, CO and H2 is favoured on smaller Cu particles (< 3 nm), whereas hydrocarbons are favoured on Cu particles in the range of 5- 15 nm [52,63]. Merino-Garcia et al. investigated product selectivity on Cu nanoparticles range from 25 to 80 nm, they found that 25 nm Cu particles favor C2H4 formation with a FE of 92.8%, attributing to higher fraction of lower coordination sites [64]. However, there are few study on the effect of ZnO particle size on the CO2 reduction activity. It seems that any structure sensitivity of ZnO particle size for CO evolution can have been masked by enhanced H2 formation. For HER, when isolating the ZnO particle size effect by comparing only those catalysts with similar size, it seems that a higher copper content in the ZnO slightly suppresses H2 evolution. H2 Tafel slopes increase with copper content when the crystallite size is constant, as indicated by the arrow in Fig. 8c. A higher Tafel slope means the current is less sensitive to a change in potential, which can result in a lower reaction rate. The sensitivity of the H2 Tafel slope to copper may be caused by a suppression of HER due to enhanced ECR. It can be concluded that the effects of adding Cu to ZnO on H2 evolution are twofold. With increasing Cu content in the catalyst, the ZnO particle size decreased and aspect ratio increased. On smaller particles with better wetting of the carbon, HER was enhanced. Simultaneously, copper addition resulted in insertion of Cu in ZnO, which suppressed hydrogen formation. By changing the reduction temperature, the particle morphology changed. Thus, the reduction temperature also influences H2 production through the size effect. An important finding is that structure and composition influence HER and ECR differently, which makes it possible to tune the formation of synthesis gas further.
Fig. 5. Aqueous CO2 electrochemical reduction with a series of CuxZn1-xOCNT catalysts with varying Cu content, reduced in H2 atmosphere at 300 °C or 350 °C.

sections.heading: 3.2.3. Catalyst stability
sections.text:
To test the stability of ZnO and Cu, chronopotentiometric test at 2.92mA/cm2 was performed for 4 h with three different catalysts, i.e. Pure ZnO/CNT catalyst and Cu/ZnO/CNT with 7 wt% and 12wt% copper loading, respectively, as shown in Fig. 9. The Cu/ZnO/CNT catalysts were prepared by impregnation of copper on ZnO/CNT, and the loading of ZnO on the CNTs was all constant at 20 wt% prepared by a modified pechini method. X-ray analysis in Fig. 9 shows the presence of crystalline copper in the copper-impregnated catalysts, which enables the study of the stability of catalysts with a segregated Cu phase on ZnO. CO formation decreased and H2 evolution increased with time for all the catalysts, but at a different rate. After 3 h, the ZnO/CNT catalyst retained 81% of its initial activity for CO evolution. The catalysts with a 7 and 12wt % crystalline copper phase retained only 65% and 19% of the CO evolution activity respectively. With these results, it is clearly revealed that the deactivation rate of the CO2 reduction to CO increased significantly with presence of crystalline copper, which also indicates that ZnO is more resistant to deactivation than copper. There could be several deactivation mechanisms: Cu sintering, active site blockage, catalyst detachment or change in catalyst selectivity. Given the fact that the H2 evolution activity remain the same, only CO formation activity decrease. We can exclude Cu sintering or catalyst detachment as the main reason for deactivation. In addition, we did not observe catalyst detachment to the solution on CuZnOCNT catalyst. Therefore, we suspect, it might be some reaction intermediates block the sites for CO formation or change in catalyst selectivity. Detailed products analysis is required to clarify whether it is due to change in
selectivity. Further studies are required and beyond the scope of the study. For further processing of syngas to valuable products, i.e. Fischer-Tropsch synthesis, a varying H2:CO ratio is a challenge. Thus, a lower copper content is beneficial for this purpose.

sections.heading: 4. Conclusions
sections.text:
In this work, CuxZn1-xOCNT catalysts have been prepared by deposition of Zn and Cu together on CNTs by impregnation with a metalcomplex solution, with copper fractions from 0 to 50 at% (Cu+Zn=100 at%). The fraction of added copper influences the catalyst morphology and chemical composition. A crystalline metallic copper phase segregates as the copper content is increased to 14, 25 and 50 at%. Also, with copper the ZnO particle size is smaller and wetting of the CNT surface by ZnO is improved. In addition, the temperature for catalyst reduction also influences morphology and composition. At 300 °C, with low copper contents, a bimodal particle size distribution is formed with some particles around 12 nm in size, and other very small particles in a film-like layer on the CNT support. When the reduction temperature is increased to 350 °C, the film layer grows into small particles, and the larger particles breaks up also making small particles. HER and ECR have different sensitivity to catalyst particle size and composition. When the catalysts are tested for electrochemical CO2 reduction in 0.1M KHCO3, it is seen that the presence of Cu in the ZnO structure enhances CO formation. The enhanced CO formation from the Cu-Zn synergy suppresses hydrogen formation slightly. The optimal amount of copper is around 14 at%, where the synergy effect is high,
Fig. 7. Energy and faradaic efficiency for CH4 and syngas on Cu14Zn86OCNT and Cu50Zn50OCNT. The error bars are calculated from the standard deviation of several GC samples taken during each 30min segment.
but before a significant amount of metallic copper has segregated. Metallic copper deactivates at a higher rate and improves the activity especially for H2, and hydrocarbons rather than CO. By comparing literature values for CO binding strength, the copper doping on ZnO seems to be able to shift the ECR activity towards CO formation closer to the top of the volcano.
HER activity shows clear particle size dependence, and is improved on smaller ZnO particles. This might be due to more low coordinated ZnO sites which can favor water adsorption and dissociation, and better electronic conductivity. Compared to HER, ECR is insensitive to the particle size in the size range examined. The CuxZn1-xOCNT catalysts show better activity for syngas with a 1:1 composition, than
